note: Claim records for physics. status: drafted = written with sources linked; verified = an independent check confirmed the source supports the claim; reviewed = a named human expert signed off.

events.when: 3rd century BCE (often given as c. 240 BCE)
events.text: Eratosthenes estimates Earth’s circumference by comparing the Sun’s angle at noon in Syene and Alexandria.

sources.cite: APS News, This Month in Physics History: June, ca. 240 B.C., Eratosthenes measures the Earth
Linda Hall Library, Scientist of the Day: Eratosthenes of Cyrene

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Cited APS page (old URL still loads) plus Linda Hall Library Scientist of the Day Corrected after this check: The exact year is not known. APS gives about 240 BCE; Linda Hall Library gives about 220 BCE. A range is safer than one year.

events.text: Archimedes states the law of the lever and the principle of buoyancy.

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Britannica blocked; checked Wikipedia On Floating Bodies and standard life dates (c. 287–212 BCE) Corrected after this check: The text is right, but the works cannot be dated to one year. On Floating Bodies is thought to come from late in his life (he died in 212 BCE), so c. 250 BCE may be too early.

events.text: Ibn al-Haytham’s Book of Optics argues that vision happens when light enters the eye, and tests claims by controlled experiment.

sources.cite: Charles Burnett, Ibn al-Haytham’s Optics, Muslim Heritage

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Britannica blocked; checked Muslim Heritage (Charles Burnett), St Andrews copy of Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry, Wikipedia mirror (notes El-Bizri 1028–1038) Corrected after this check: The date is debated. The common range is 1011–1021, but historians such as Charles Burnett date the writing to 1028–1038 in Cairo, and the book appears in a list of his works that runs to 1038.

events.text: Copernicus’s On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres puts the Sun, not the Earth, at the center.
Kepler shows that planets move in ellipses and states his three laws of planetary motion.

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Smithsonian How Things Fly: first two laws in Astronomia nova (1609), third law in Harmonices Mundi (1619)

events.text: Galileo’s Sidereus Nuncius reports four moons orbiting Jupiter, seen through his telescope.
Newton’s Principia sets out the laws of motion and universal gravitation.
Volta builds the first electric battery, the voltaic pile.

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: IEEE Spectrum / APS search results: pile built 1799, announced in a letter to the Royal Society dated 20 March 1800

events.text: Sadi Carnot works out the limits on how well heat engines can turn heat into work, laying the groundwork for thermodynamics.

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Encyclopedia.com biography of Carnot (calls the 1824 work the beginning of thermodynamics) Corrected after this check: “Founding thermodynamics” overstates. Carnot’s 1824 book is usually called the beginning of the subject, but it used the wrong caloric theory of heat and the science was built later by Clapeyron, Kelvin and Clausius.

events.text: Faraday discovers electromagnetic induction, the principle behind generators and transformers.
Mayer (1842), Joule’s experiments and Helmholtz’s 1847 essay together establish the conservation of energy.

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: History-of-science text on conservation of energy (Mayer 1842, Joule 1843, Helmholtz 1847) Corrected after this check: Credit is incomplete. Julius Robert Mayer stated the idea in 1842, before Joule’s 1843 results and Helmholtz’s 1847 essay; histories usually name all three.

events.text: Maxwell’s “A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field” unites electricity, magnetism and light.

sources.cite: Maxwell, Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society 155 (1865)

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: DOI resolves to the 1865 Phil. Trans. paper (Royal Society Making Science record and search results)

events.text: The Michelson–Morley experiment finds no sign of the “ether” that light was thought to travel through.
Röntgen discovers X-rays.

sources.cite: Nobel Prize in Physics 1901, Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Nobel 1901 facts page (via search); Röntgen’s discovery of 8 November 1895 is standard

checked.method: Nobel 1903 summary; Becquerel 1896, polonium and radium announced July and December 1898

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Nobel 1906 facts page; 1897 discovery is standard

events.text: Einstein publishes papers on light quanta (the photoelectric effect), Brownian motion, special relativity and E = mc².

sources.cite: Nobel Prize in Physics 1921, Albert Einstein
Physics World, Five papers that shook the world

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Physics World “Five papers that shook the world” lists all four topics; the cited Nobel page only covers the photoelectric effect, so a second source is added

events.text: Rutherford shows that an atom’s mass is concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
Einstein completes general relativity: gravity is the curvature of spacetime.

Two British eclipse expeditions, organized by Frank Dyson and Arthur Eddington, measure starlight bending around the Sun. Eddington’s team observed from Príncipe and another team from Sobral, Brazil. The results support general relativity.

sources.cite: Dyson, Eddington and Davidson, Philosophical Transactions A 220 (1920)

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Wikipedia (Eddington experiment, via mirror); DOI checked via ADS/Zenodo records of the 1920 paper Corrected after this check: Dyson did not lead an expedition. As Astronomer Royal he organized the project with Eddington. Eddington and Cottingham went to Príncipe; Crommelin and Davidson went to Sobral, Brazil.

events.text: Heisenberg, Schrödinger, Born, Dirac and others formulate quantum mechanics; Heisenberg states the uncertainty principle (1927).

sources.cite: Nobel Prize in Physics 1932, Werner Heisenberg

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Nobel 1932 facts page; 1925–1927 development of matrix and wave mechanics and the 1927 uncertainty principle are standard

events.text: Hubble shows that more distant galaxies are moving away faster, using many speeds measured by Vesto Slipher. Georges Lemaître had predicted this in 1927. It is evidence that the universe is expanding.

sources.cite: Hubble, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 15 (1929)
Cambridge University Press, Renaming Hubble’s Law to the Hubble-Lemaître Law

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: DOI checked via ADS/PMC record; arXiv 1809.02557 and Cambridge University Press article on the IAU 2018 resolution Corrected after this check: Credit is incomplete. Georges Lemaître predicted and estimated this relation in 1927, and many of the speeds came from Vesto Slipher’s measurements. The IAU in 2018 recommended the name Hubble–Lemaître law.

sources.cite: Nobel Prize in Physics 1935, James Chadwick

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Nobel 1935 facts page; February 1932 discovery is standard

events.text: Hahn and Strassmann split uranium; Meitner and Frisch explain it as nuclear fission.

sources.cite: Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1944, Otto Hahn

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Atomic Heritage Foundation profile: Hahn and Strassmann’s barium finding (Dec 1938), Meitner and Frisch’s explanation and the word “fission” (Nature, Feb 1939). Credit split is fair.

events.text: The first nuclear weapon is tested at Trinity, New Mexico (16 July); atomic bombs destroy Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August.

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Search results from OSTI Manhattan Project history, NPS Trinity Site, Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center: 16 July 1945; Hiroshima 6 Aug, Nagasaki 9 Aug

events.text: John Bardeen and Walter Brattain build the first transistor at Bell Labs, in a group led by William Shockley, who soon designed an improved version. All three share the 1956 Nobel Prize. Transistors are the basis of modern electronics.

sources.cite: Computer History Museum, 1947: Invention of the Point-Contact Transistor

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Computer History Museum Silicon Engine timeline (1947 point-contact transistor; 1948 junction transistor) Corrected after this check: The first transistor (December 1947) was built by Bardeen and Brattain. Shockley led the group and invented the junction transistor soon after (1948). All three shared the 1956 Nobel.

events.text: Chien-Shiung Wu’s experiment shows that the weak force does not respect mirror symmetry (parity).

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Wikipedia Wu experiment (mirror) and APS Lee–Yang history: asymmetry seen December 1956, published 1957; Lee and Yang proposed the test (could be mentioned)

checked.method: Nobel 1978 summary and search results: detected 1964, published 1965; Big Bang interpretation by Dicke, Peebles and colleagues

events.text: Jocelyn Bell Burnell discovers the first pulsar, a rapidly spinning neutron star.

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Linda Hall Library: first pulsar confirmed 28 November 1967 while she was a Cambridge graduate student (in Antony Hewish’s group)

events.text: Two teams studying distant supernovae find that the universe’s expansion is accelerating.

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Nobel 2011 press materials (via search): two teams, results in 1998

events.text: The ATLAS and CMS experiments at CERN announce a new particle (4 July). By March 2013 more data confirm it is a Higgs boson.

sources.cite: CERN, The birth of the Higgs boson

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: CERN page “The birth of the Higgs boson” (cited CERN page not reachable) Corrected after this check: Slight overstatement. On 4 July 2012 the experiments announced a new particle that looked like the Higgs boson; CERN says it was confirmed as a Higgs boson in March 2013.

checked.method: LIGO press release: detected 14 September 2015 (09:51 UTC), announced 11 February 2016, Physical Review Letters

events.text: The US National Ignition Facility achieves fusion ignition (5 December, announced 13 December): the fuel gives off more energy (3.15 MJ) than the laser light that hit it (2.05 MJ). The lasers themselves used far more electricity than that, so it is not yet a power source.

sources.cite: US Department of Energy announcement, December 2022
Physics Today, National Ignition Facility surpasses long-awaited fusion milestone

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: University of California / LLNL release (DOE text) and Physics Today news story (300 MJ grid figure) Corrected after this check: “More energy than the lasers put in” is misleading. The shot made 3.15 MJ of fusion energy from 2.05 MJ of laser light reaching the target, but the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the power grid. Also note the result was announced 13 December.

events.text: The Nobel Prize in Physics honors Clarke, Devoret and Martinis for showing quantum tunnelling and quantized energy in an electric circuit large enough to hold in your hand.

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Prize motivation via Physics Today; “big enough to be held in the hand” is the Academy’s own phrase (via Lindau and Scroll). Experiments were done in 1984–85, which could be added.

people.name: Ibn al-Haytham
people.text: Pioneered experimental optics and the idea that theories must be tested.

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: St Andrews DSB entry (b. 965, d. Cairo c. 1040) and Wikipedia mirror (born Basra)

people.name: Shen Kuo
people.text: Gave the first clear description of the magnetic compass needle and noticed that it does not point exactly north–south (magnetic declination).

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Wikipedia Shen Kuo (1031–1095; Dream Pool Essays 1088) and AAAS Scientia article Corrected after this check: Small precision fix. Shen Kuo wrote that the needle points south but is always a little east of due south. Saying it does not point exactly north–south matches his words and is still correct.

people.name: Emmy Noether
people.text: Proved that every continuous symmetry of nature corresponds to a conserved quantity (Noether’s theorem).

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Colloquium “A Century of Noether’s Theorem” (arXiv 1902.01989); years from standard references Corrected after this check: Overstates: the theorem covers continuous symmetries (like shifting in time or space), not every symmetry. Also she worked in the United States from 1933 until her death.

people.name: Lise Meitner
people.text: Co-explained nuclear fission; left out of the 1944 Nobel Prize awarded to her colleague Otto Hahn.

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Atomic Heritage Foundation profile (b. 7 Nov 1878 Vienna; d. 27 Oct 1968 Cambridge) Corrected after this check: Region leaves out Germany, where she did her main work (Berlin, 1907–1938) before fleeing to Sweden. Years and text are correct.

people.name: C. V. Raman
people.text: Discovered that when light scatters off molecules, a tiny part of it changes color (the Raman effect); Nobel Prize 1930.

checked.by: independent AI fact-check (separate agent, not a human expert)
checked.method: Nobel 1930 facts page (via search) and standard references Corrected after this check: Slight overstatement: only a tiny part of the scattered light changes color (wavelength).
